parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A woman reports a stolen bicycle to the police.
script: Good afternoon. How can I help?
Hello. I'd like to report that my bicycle has been stolen.
I'm sorry to hear that. Can I take your name?
Olivia Price. P, R, I, C, E.
Flat six, Cedar House, on Brook Lane.
Thank you. Can you describe the bike? What make is it?
It's a Voyager. V, O, Y, A, G, E, R.
What type of bike is it?
A mountain bike, although I mostly use it in the city.
From outside the gym on Park Street. I was inside for a couple of hours.
I left it there at six p.m. and when I came out at eight, it was gone.
Yes, with a cable lock. I found the lock on the ground. It had been cut.
Is there anything that would help us identify it?
Yes, it has a basket on the front, which isn't very common on mountain bikes.
That's useful. Your crime reference number is C R four four seven one. Please quote it if you contact us again or speak to your insurance company.

groups.instr: Complete the report form below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

items.q: Distinctive feature: a ____ on the front

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A hall warden explains the rules and facilities of a student residence.
script: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to Riverside Hall. I'm Mrs Dunn, the warden, and I'd like to go through a few important points.
First, quiet hours. From eleven p.m. until seven a.m., please keep noise to a minimum. Many students have early lectures.
You're welcome to have guests, but all guests must sign in at reception when they arrive. This is for fire safety reasons, so we know who's in the building.
Speaking of fire safety, the fire alarm is tested every Wednesday morning at ten. If it rings at any other time, leave the building immediately.
Your shared kitchens are cleaned by our cleaners twice a week, but please wash your own dishes. Your own rooms are your responsibility.
Now, the facilities. The laundry room is open twenty-four hours a day, and you pay using the app.
The gym is open from eight a.m. to eight p.m., and you'll need to complete a short induction before using it.
The music practice room has the same hours as the gym, from eight until eight, so that it doesn't disturb people at night.
The bike store is open twenty-four hours, and you'll be given an access card.
The games room is closed at the moment while it's being redecorated. It should reopen next month.
And the cinema room is open at weekends only, when we show films on Friday and Saturday evenings and Sunday afternoons.

groups.instr: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

items.q: When is the fire alarm tested?

groups.instr: When is each facility available? Choose A, B, C or D. You may use any letter more than once.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students, Sana and Nico, plan a podcast series about climate solutions.
script: Sana, let's finalise the plan for our podcast series.
OK. I think we agreed that the aim is to show practical solutions to climate change, rather than just how bad things are. People are tired of bad news.
Exactly. How long should each episode be?
Twenty minutes. Long enough for a proper conversation, short enough for a commute.
Who should be our first guest?
I'd like to start with the farmer we met who uses solar-powered pumps for irrigation. It's a great story.
Good choice. One problem with our test recording, though: there was a terrible echo in the room.
We should record in the media centre studio next time. And we'll publish the episodes on the university radio website.
Let's confirm the guests for each episode. 'Feeding the Future' is the farmer, of course.
For 'Power to the People', about community energy, we've got the engineer from the solar cooperative.
'Green Investment' will be with the economist from the business school.
'Heat and Hearts' is about how rising temperatures affect health, so the doctor from the city hospital.
And 'Lessons for Tomorrow' will be with the teacher who started the school garden project.

groups.instr: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

items.q: What is the aim of the podcast?
options: to explain the science of climate change

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on how migrating birds find their way.
script: Today we're going to look at one of the great mysteries of biology: how migrating birds find their way across thousands of kilometres.

The distances can be extraordinary. The Arctic tern travels from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back each year, covering around seventy thousand kilometres. In 2022, a young bar-tailed godwit was tracked flying non-stop for eleven days from Alaska to Tasmania, without eating or resting.

How do they navigate? We know that many birds can detect the Earth's magnetic field. One theory is that a molecule in their eyes, called cryptochrome, may allow them to actually see the magnetic field as a pattern.
Birds also use the sun and the stars. Young birds making their first migration seem to rely largely on instinct, inheriting a basic direction and distance from their parents.

A famous experiment in the 1950s illustrated this. Starlings caught in the Netherlands during migration were taken by plane to Switzerland and released. Adult birds corrected their course and reached their usual winter grounds, but young birds simply continued in their original direction and ended up in the wrong place.
Homing pigeons use additional cues, including smell. Pigeons that cannot smell have much more difficulty finding their way home.
Unfortunately, human activity is making migration harder. Light pollution in cities can disorient birds flying at night, causing many to collide with buildings.
Climate change also causes problems. Some birds now arrive at their breeding grounds too late, after the peak in insect food has passed, a problem known as mismatch.
Our knowledge is improving rapidly, thanks to tiny tracking tags, some weighing less than a gram, which allow scientists to follow even small songbirds.

passages.title: The First Flight
paragraphs: On 17 December 1903, on a windswept beach near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville Wright lay on the lower wing of a fragile wooden aircraft as it rose into the air. The flight lasted just 12 seconds and covered about 37 metres, but it was the first controlled, sustained flight of a powered aircraft carrying a person.

Orville and his brother Wilbur were not trained engineers. They ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio, where they designed, built and repaired bicycles. Their interest in flight was inspired partly by the work of the German glider pioneer Otto Lilienthal, who made thousands of glider flights before he was killed in a crash in 1896. Rather than discouraging the brothers, Lilienthal's death convinced them that the key problem was control.

The Wrights took a methodical approach. When they found that published data on wing shapes was unreliable, they built their own wind tunnel in 1901 and tested around 200 different wing designs. They also developed a system called wing warping, in which the edges of the wings could be twisted to control the aircraft's balance, much as birds adjust their wings. Combined with a movable rudder, this gave the pilot control in all three directions.

They chose Kitty Hawk for their experiments because it had steady winds and soft sand for landings, and because it was remote enough to work in privacy. Their aircraft, the Flyer, was powered by a lightweight petrol engine they had designed and built with their mechanic, Charlie Taylor, because no suitable engine was available.

On that December day, the brothers made four flights. The longest, piloted by Wilbur, lasted 59 seconds and covered 260 metres. Remarkably, few newspapers took any notice, and some that did reported the event inaccurately. Many people simply did not believe that powered flight had been achieved.

It was only in 1908, when Wilbur gave public demonstrations in France and Orville in the United States, that the world was convinced. Crowds were astonished by the control the Wrights displayed, turning and circling with ease. Within a few years, aircraft were being built across Europe and America, and the age of aviation had truly begun.

The brothers became wealthy from selling aircraft.

passages.title: The Rise of Resistant Bacteria
paragraphs: When Alexander Fleming accepted the Nobel Prize in 1945 for the discovery of penicillin, he used his speech to issue a warning. If people took too little of the drug, or stopped taking it too early, he said, bacteria could learn to resist it. Within a few years, his warning had come true, as resistant strains of bacteria began to appear in hospitals.

Resistance develops through natural selection. When bacteria are exposed to an antibiotic, most are killed, but a few may carry genetic changes that allow them to survive. These survivors multiply, and soon a resistant population has developed. Bacteria can also pass genes for resistance directly to one another, even between different species, which allows resistance to spread rapidly.

The misuse of antibiotics has greatly accelerated the problem. Doctors in many countries have prescribed antibiotics for viral infections such as colds, against which they have no effect. In some countries, antibiotics can be bought without a prescription. In agriculture, antibiotics have been widely given to healthy animals, not to treat disease but to make them grow faster, and in some countries farming accounts for the majority of antibiotic use.

The consequences are serious. A major study published in 2022 estimated that, in 2019, around 1.27 million deaths worldwide were directly caused by infections resistant to antibiotics, more than were caused by HIV or malaria. Without action, experts warn, routine operations and treatments such as chemotherapy could become far more dangerous, since they depend on antibiotics to prevent infections.

Despite the threat, few new antibiotics are being developed. For pharmaceutical companies, antibiotics are less profitable than other drugs, because they are taken for short periods and new ones are kept in reserve and used as little as possible to slow the development of resistance. Many large companies have abandoned antibiotic research altogether.

There are, however, reasons for hope. Hospitals are improving 'stewardship', making sure antibiotics are used only when necessary. Researchers are reviving phage therapy, which uses viruses that infect and kill specific bacteria. And in 2020, scientists at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology used artificial intelligence to identify a powerful new antibiotic, which they named halicin, after the computer in the film 2001: A Space Odyssey.

passages.title: Should Voting Be Compulsory?
paragraphs: In most democracies, voting is a right but not a duty. In a small number of countries, however, citizens are legally required to vote. Belgium has the oldest such system still in operation, dating from 1893, and Australia introduced compulsory voting for national elections in 1924. Today, more than twenty countries have some form of compulsory voting, although not all of them enforce it.

The effect on turnout is striking. In Australia, more than 90 percent of registered voters regularly take part in national elections, compared with figures of around 60 percent in many countries where voting is voluntary. Australians who fail to vote without a valid reason receive a modest fine of around 20 Australian dollars.

Supporters argue that compulsory voting makes governments more legitimate, since they are chosen by almost the entire population rather than by a self-selected minority. They also point out that in voluntary systems, young people and those on low incomes are much less likely to vote than older and wealthier citizens, so their interests may receive less attention from politicians. When everyone votes, parties cannot win simply by mobilising their most committed supporters, and some researchers believe this encourages more moderate campaigns that appeal to a broad range of voters.

Opponents argue that forcing people to vote is a restriction on individual freedom, and that choosing not to vote can itself be a form of political expression. They also worry that compulsory voting brings uninterested and uninformed voters to the polls. In Australia, a small proportion of voters cast what is known as a 'donkey vote', simply numbering the candidates in the order in which they appear on the ballot paper, which may slightly favour candidates listed first.

Some critics also note that compulsory voting does not solve the deeper reasons why people feel disconnected from politics, such as distrust of politicians or a sense that their vote makes no difference.

On balance, I believe the advantages of compulsory voting outweigh the disadvantages, provided that two conditions are met. First, fines should be small, so that the system encourages rather than punishes. Second, ballot papers should include a 'none of the above' option, allowing citizens to take part while rejecting all candidates. In this way, compulsory voting can strengthen democracy without forcing anyone to support a party they do not believe in.

groups.instr: Do the following statements agree with the views of the writer in Reading Passage 3? Choose YES, NO or NOT GIVEN.

items.q: Australia introduced compulsory voting in the 1920s.
Belgium was the first country in history to make voting compulsory.
Low-income citizens are less likely to vote in voluntary systems.
Compulsory voting leads to more extreme politicians.
Voters should be allowed to reject all the candidates.

groups.instr: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

items.q: What happens to Australians who do not vote without a good reason?
options: They lose the right to vote.
a vote for the smallest party.
numbering candidates in the order they are listed.

items.q: What is the writer's overall view?
options: Compulsory voting is acceptable with certain conditions.

task1.text: The bar chart below shows the average size, in square metres, of newly built houses in five countries in 2000 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
model: The bar chart compares the average floor area of newly built houses in Australia, the USA, Denmark, Japan and the UK in 2000 and 2020.

Overall, there were large differences between the countries, with new homes in Australia and the USA being more than twice the size of those in Japan and the UK. Changes over the twenty-year period were relatively small in every country.

In 2000, Australia had the largest new houses, at 227 square metres on average, followed closely by the USA at 200. Danish homes were considerably smaller, at 130 square metres, while new houses in Japan averaged 100 square metres and those in the UK just 80, the smallest of the five countries.

By 2020, the average size of new homes in Australia had fallen to 214 square metres, although it remained the largest. The figure for the USA was almost unchanged, at 201. Denmark was the only other country to see an increase, to 137 square metres, while new homes in Japan and the UK became slightly smaller, at 95 and 76 square metres respectively.

task2.text: Some people believe that governments should spend more money on public transport than on building new roads. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Write at least 250 words.
model: As cities grow, governments must decide how to spend limited transport budgets. Some argue that money should go mainly to building and widening roads, while others believe public transport should be the priority. I strongly agree that investment in public transport should come first, although some spending on roads will always be necessary.

The main argument for public transport is efficiency. A single bus or train can carry dozens or hundreds of people using far less space than the cars they replace. Building more roads, by contrast, often fails to reduce congestion in the long term, because new road space encourages more people to drive, a phenomenon known as induced demand. Within a few years, the new roads can be just as crowded as the old ones.

Public transport also brings environmental and social benefits. It produces far lower emissions per passenger than private cars, helping to reduce air pollution and carbon emissions. It is also essential for people who cannot drive or afford a car, including many young people, elderly people and those on low incomes. Good public transport therefore helps people reach jobs, education and healthcare.

On the other hand, roads remain important. Buses, delivery vehicles and emergency services all depend on them, and in rural areas public transport may never be practical for many journeys. Existing roads also need regular maintenance to remain safe.

In conclusion, while roads must be maintained and improved where necessary, I believe that governments should prioritise public transport, because it moves people more efficiently, reduces pollution and makes cities fairer and more accessible for everyone.

speaking.cue:
Describe a time when you lost something important.
You should say:
- what you lost
- where you lost it
- how you tried to find it
and explain how you felt about it.
speaking.cueModel: I'd like to talk about the time I lost my wallet on a bus in Dhaka during my first year at university. It wasn't just the money that worried me. My student ID card, my national ID card and my bank card were all inside. I realised it was missing as soon as I got off the bus, and my heart sank. At first, I panicked and ran after the bus, but of course it was impossible to catch it in the traffic. Then I tried to think calmly. I called my bank straight away to block the card, and a friend helped me find the bus company's phone number online. I called them and gave them the bus number, which luckily I'd noticed. They said they would ask the driver. For two days, I heard nothing, and I'd almost given up hope. Then I got a call saying the conductor had found my wallet under a seat and handed it in. When I collected it, everything was still there, even the money. I was incredibly relieved and grateful. I tried to give the conductor some money as a thank-you, but he refused. It taught me to be more careful, but it also restored my faith in people.
